heading: PROPHET ISMĀʿĪL (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ)
title: TRUE TO HIS PROMISE
themes: Trust • Responsible Effort • Truthfulness • Patience • Family • Worship
scope: 6 CONNECTED STORIES | 10 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 20 SELECTED AYĀT
reviewNote: Qualified scholarly, muṣḥaf, linguistic, accessibility and child-safety review required before publication
introduction: This is the eighth world of ʿIBRAH Junior, developed for the Imaan & Akhlaq educational ecosystem. It follows the earlier worlds on Ādam, Idrīs, Nūḥ, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Ibrāhīm and Lūṭ (peace be upon them). The adult ʿIBRAH Volume Eight is arranged into three principal movements: the infant Ismāʿīl and the care and provision surrounding Hājar and Zamzam; Ismāʿīl’s own truthful and patient prophetic character; and his cooperation with Ibrāhīm in raising the Sacred House’s foundations. These movements govern this children’s adaptation.

The six fictional Imaan-and-Akhlaq stories follow the family, Sheikh Uncle’s Academy, and Team Amanah through a “Promise Project.” The familiar compass appears only as an ordinary storytelling object. Modern dialogue, classroom models, family situations and ethical dilemmas are newly created educational applications, never scenes inserted into Prophetic history. The historical narration must be sourced from the Qur’an and authenticated Sunnah; classical Tafsir may explain but must never be mistaken for the words of revelation.

stories.title: The Water That Was Not There
stories.subtitle: A family plan and a story of Hājar

blocks.text: The morning after the school holidays began, Akhlaq noticed a blue folder on the dining table. On its cover, Imaan had written in careful letters: THE PROMISE PROJECT. Beside the folder lay the old brass compass from Sheikh Uncle's library, now safely kept in its case. The compass was an ordinary object, but the children had made its marks into reminders of the lessons they had studied about Prophet Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him.

“Does this folder point to the next world?” Akhlaq asked. Imaan shook her head. “It points to the cupboard. Ammi asked us to prepare supplies for Dadi Jaan's visitors.” Akhlaq peered inside. There were lists of cups, clean towels and water bottles. “This is not nearly as mysterious as I hoped.”

A little later, the house tap ran weakly and stopped. Salaam came from the kitchen and explained that the neighborhood water supply had been interrupted. Drinking water had been stored safely, but the family needed to manage it carefully until the supply returned. Akhlaq looked disappointed. They had planned to water the garden and wash their bicycles that afternoon.

Salamah asked Imaan and Akhlaq to help put the drinking water somewhere easy for Dadi to reach. Their cousins Mohsin and Mohsina arrived while the children were counting bottles. Mohsin said, “If we are patient, perhaps the water will come back by itself.” Imaan replied, “We can be patient and still carry the bottles.”

Dadi Jaan heard the exchange. She sat with them and opened the Qur'an to the prayer of Ibrāhīm for the family he had settled near the Sacred House (Ibrāhīm 14:37). Then she told them that the authentic narration in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī describes Hājar in the valley of Makkah with her infant Ismāʿīl. When their available water ran out, she did not stop caring for her child or simply wait without effort. She searched for help and water, moving between Ṣafā and Marwah. Allah granted the blessing of Zamzam.

“Was Hājar supposed to find water in exactly seven minutes?” Akhlaq asked. “No,” Dadi answered. “Do not invent times the report does not give. And do not turn her extraordinary situation into permission to put children in danger. In our home, adults make sure children have water and safety.”
Mohsina looked at the supply folder. “So trusting Allah is not an excuse for doing nothing.” Dadi nodded. “It is a reason to do what is right while relying upon Him.”

For the rest of the morning, the children helped with small, safe tasks: arranging cups, recording what had been used, and setting aside water for guests. When the supply finally returned that evening, Akhlaq did not race to the garden hose. Instead, he wrote on the first page of the folder: TRUST IN ALLAH. THEN TAKE RESPONSIBLE ACTION.
Underneath the sentence, he found a note Sheikh Uncle had placed there earlier: THE NEXT QUESTION IS NOT ONLY HOW A CHILD IS CARED FOR, BUT HOW A CHILD LEARNS TO CARE.

stories.title: Seven Steps of Determination
stories.subtitle: Planning without pretending to recreate history

blocks.text: At Sheikh Uncle's Academy, the children were preparing a small charity exhibition. Their class had agreed to create a display about water, gratitude and the caring work that keeps communities healthy. Mohsina had gathered pictures of wells and water tanks. Mohsin wanted to build a cardboard model with moving parts. Akhlaq wanted the model to have a flashing light, a bell and, if the teacher agreed, a tiny fountain.

Sir Zameer listened to the plan. “You have described an exciting display,” he said. “Have you described who will build it, how long it will take, or how you will check that the information is correct?” The four children went silent. Their enthusiasm had arrived before their organization.

Then Imaan remembered Dadi's story about Hājar. “She trusted Allah and searched for water. We should not just hope our display builds itself.” Sir Zameer nodded, but cautioned them that a school project was not comparable to the danger Hājar faced with her infant. “You can learn a habit of responsible effort,” he said, “without claiming to relive that sacred history.”

Together they wrote seven ordinary project steps: decide the purpose, check the sources, divide the jobs, use safe materials, test the model, listen to feedback, and present the result honestly. The number seven helped the children remember their plan, but it was explicitly their own classroom mnemonic, not a new religious ritual or a reconstruction of the route between Ṣafā and Marwah.

On the first day Mohsin's model collapsed. He was tempted to hide it and borrow another team's design. Mohsina reminded him that a failed model was useful information, not a shameful verdict. They made the base wider. On the second attempt, the cardboard held but the labels were missing. Imaan rewrote them in larger letters. Akhlaq tested whether a younger student could understand the display without an adult explaining every word.

Their final model was simple: a river, a family home, a storage tank and a clear panel that explained why drinking water must be protected. A separate reading card explained that Allah honored Hājar's efforts and provided Zamzam in the account preserved by the Prophet's Sunnah. Sir Zameer asked the children what part had been hardest.

“Not giving up after the first failed test,” said Mohsin. “Sharing the work,” said Mohsina. “Not adding the fountain,” Akhlaq admitted. “It would have looked brilliant,” he added, “but somebody would have to clean up the water.”

On exhibition day, a visitor complimented the model's usefulness. Akhlaq looked toward the old compass sitting next to the display and smiled. The journey's second mark was not about spectacle. It was about continuing honest work even when the first idea was not the best one.
Sheikh Uncle, passing by, placed another note on the desk: A PROMISE IS NOT ONLY SOMETHING WE SAY. IT IS SOMETHING SOMEONE ELSE LEARNS TO TRUST.

stories.title: The Notebook of Promises
stories.subtitle: What happens when someone counts on your word

blocks.text: The Promise Project acquired its name for a reason. During the exhibition, Imaan had promised a younger class that she would return the borrowed books by Wednesday. Akhlaq had promised Mohsin to help repair one loose corner of the model. Mohsina promised to bring fresh labels, and Mohsin promised the teacher that the display would be returned to the equipment cupboard safely.

By Tuesday afternoon, Akhlaq had completely forgotten his promise. A new football game had been arranged, and he was excited to play. When Mohsin reminded him about the model, he sighed. “It is just one corner. You could fix it without me.” Mohsin did not sound angry, but he looked disappointed. “I can,” he replied. “I waited because you said we would do it together.”

At home, Akhlaq found the blue folder on the table. Dadi Jaan had added a new page headed: WHO IS WAITING FOR MY WORD? There were four empty lines. “You are making a list of everything I said this week?” Akhlaq asked. “Not everything,” Dadi said. “Only the promises important enough that somebody may rely upon them.”

Dadi then read the Qur'anic description of Prophet Ismāʿīl in Sūrat Maryam 19:54. Allah calls him truthful to his promise and identifies him as a messenger and a prophet. The verse did not need an invented tale about an appointment or an impossible waiting period to make its praise meaningful. His reputation for faithfulness was itself remarkable.

Imaan asked, “Does keeping a promise mean I can never change a plan?” Dadi explained that unexpected illness, emergencies and unavoidable changes can happen. A trustworthy person communicates honestly and tries to repair the inconvenience. Akhlaq asked whether a promise to do something wrong must still be kept. “No,” she answered. “A person must never carry out a wrong act merely because they promised it. Ask for help and correct the promise.”

That evening Akhlaq called Mohsin. “I forgot,” he admitted. “I should have told you earlier. Can I come now, or would tomorrow morning be better?” Mohsin suggested the morning. Akhlaq wrote the time in his notebook and placed the book beside his school bag.

On Wednesday he arrived when he said he would. The work took only fifteen minutes. While they taped the model, Mohsin said, “It is not the corner that bothered me. I was wondering whether you meant what you said.” Akhlaq felt the weight of those words. A promise could be small in size and still large in another person's heart.
At the end of the day, Akhlaq wrote in the folder: WHEN MY WORD IS TRUSTWORTHY, I MAKE LIFE EASIER FOR OTHERS. Imaan added a note below it: DO NOT PROMISE WHAT YOU CANNOT RESPONSIBLY DO.
The next page of the folder had an unexpected heading: THE FAMILY CLOCK.

The family clock had stopped working. It sat above the bookshelf in the living room, pointing permanently to a quarter past five. Akhlaq noticed the problem when he tried to use it as evidence that the evening was still young. Salamah glanced at the real time and smiled. “That clock is not going to excuse you from putting away the game.”

Salaam took the clock down so he could replace its battery. While he worked, the children talked about their changing routines. Mohsin said that sometimes homework, sport and play felt as though they all arrived together. Mohsina said that a reminder helped, provided it was not shouted from the other side of the house. Imaan admitted that she was good at organizing plans but could sound impatient when everyone else moved more slowly.

Dadi Jaan opened the Qur'an to Maryam 19:55. Allah praises Ismāʿīl because he used to instruct his family about prayer and zakāh, and he was pleasing to his Lord. This was not merely a lesson about knowing religious rules. It showed a household in which acts of worship and care mattered enough to be remembered and encouraged.

“Then the app should send a loud alarm every minute until everyone prays,” Akhlaq suggested. Imaan gave him a look. “That would encourage people to throw away their phones.” Dadi laughed. “Reminders should support worship, not make children feel watched or humiliated.” She explained that the actual obligations must be taught accurately according to age and family guidance. The children were learning how to speak gently, prepare in good time and help rather than criticize one another.

They agreed to try a simple family routine that evening. The board beside the bookshelf would list schoolwork, family help and space for salah reminders. The children could choose their own helpful tasks. Imaan would put the prayer mats neatly away after they were used. Akhlaq would clear the path near Dadi's room so nobody tripped over school bags. Mohsina volunteered to check whether the younger cousins had a quiet place to finish homework. Mohsin offered to remind his brother kindly about an agreed responsibility rather than shout from the stairs.

The plan did not proceed perfectly. Akhlaq forgot his task until Salamah asked him once. Imaan began to tell him what he should have done, then stopped. “I was about to turn a reminder into a lecture,” she said. Akhlaq grinned. “That would have been a very long lecture.”

After dinner, Salaam fitted the battery and put the clock back on the wall. Its hands began moving again. He asked the children what the clock had taught them. “That being right about the time is not enough,” Imaan answered. “How we help each other matters too.”
The folder's next page contained a question in large letters: WHEN THE RIGHT THING IS DIFFICULT, CAN WE STILL CHOOSE TRUST AND OBEDIENCE?

stories.title: The Difficult Question
stories.subtitle: Learning about a great test without reenacting it

blocks.text: The question was waiting when Sheikh Uncle entered the classroom the next morning. He had brought no model, no dramatic costume and no strange prop. Only a Qur'an, a folder of references and a plain wooden bookstand.

The children had been discussing the household of Prophet Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him. This time their lesson concerned the great test described in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt 37:102–107. Sheikh Uncle told them that the Qur'an records a dream shown to Ibrāhīm, the response of his son, their submission, and Allah's declaration that the trial had been fulfilled. Allah provided a great ransom. The Qur'anic passage itself does not name the son. The widely held classical identification is Ismāʿīl, which should be identified as scholarly explanation rather than words printed in that particular verse.

Akhlaq raised his hand. “Are we supposed to prove obedience by doing something dangerous?” Sheikh Uncle answered immediately. “No. Nobody may invent such a test or imitate harm to a child. This was a unique revealed event for a Prophet. A child should never accept a demand for harm or abuse because someone claims it is a religious test. Your safety matters. Ask a trusted adult for help.”

He explained that children could still learn genuine, ordinary obedience in appropriate ways: keeping promises, speaking truthfully when it felt uncomfortable, accepting a reasonable safety instruction, and refusing to harm others. But those examples were not equivalent to the revealed trial.

That afternoon at the academy, the teachers were preparing a class service day. Team Amanah had been asked to help organize donated school supplies. A few students wanted to put their own names on the largest sign, even though many others had contributed. Akhlaq felt tempted to join them. He had spent hours preparing boxes. “Surely we deserve to be noticed,” he said.

Mohsina replied, “We can thank everyone without pretending that the project belongs to four people.” Imaan suggested putting the beneficiaries and the purpose of the project first. The team would still have a separate contributors' page. Nobody's work would be erased, but the poster would not make the project a trophy for a few names.

The choice felt uncomfortable. Then Akhlaq remembered something Sheikh Uncle had said: doing what is right can sometimes mean giving up a smaller personal desire, not putting yourself or anyone else in danger. The children changed the sign. They thanked the volunteers. They finished the work.

Before leaving, Sheikh Uncle asked them to repeat the most important safety lesson. “We learn the revealed story accurately,” Imaan said. “We do not act it out,” Mohsin added. “And nobody has permission to hurt a child,” said Mohsina. Akhlaq finished: “Ordinary responsibilities can still teach us to choose what is right.”
The folder's fifth page now bore the words: GREAT FAITH DOES NOT NEED GREAT APPLAUSE. The final page was titled: THE HOUSE THAT PEOPLE RETURN TO.

stories.title: The House That People Return To
stories.subtitle: Building something useful and praying for acceptance

blocks.text: The last day of the Promise Project began in the school courtyard. Sir Zameer had asked Team Amanah to improve the small reading corner used by younger children and visiting families. At first Akhlaq wanted a tall display board with golden letters. Mohsin suggested a trophy shelf. Mohsina wanted comfortable seating, and Imaan asked whether a younger child using a mobility aid could enter easily.

They went to work with simple materials. Salaam helped the children check the safety of the shelves. Salamah provided washable cushions. Dadi Jaan donated several carefully chosen books. Nobody was allowed to climb or use sharp tools without responsible adult supervision. The children made a wide walkway, a low book-return basket and labels large enough for beginners to read.

During the work, Dadi asked Akhlaq if he remembered another construction task from the life of Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl. “The Kaʿbah!” he said. She opened al-Baqarah 2:127. The Qur'an explicitly names Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl together as they raised the foundations of the Sacred House. It records their supplication: ‘Our Lord, accept from us.’ The purpose was obedience and worship of Allah, not personal reputation.

She explained that the Kaʿbah is uniquely sacred, and their classroom reading corner was not comparable to it in sanctity. They could learn from the humility of the builders without claiming to rebuild or simulate the House of Allah. Sheikh Uncle also reminded them that the sacred sanctuary's detailed history must come from reliable revelation and reports, not decorative guesses about its ancient appearance.

The first visitors arrived before the team had finished tying the last labels. A younger girl went straight to the low shelf and found a picture book. Another child sat near the entrance and began reading aloud. Akhlaq noticed the empty trophy shelf they had decided not to build. He was surprised that he did not miss it.

When Sir Zameer praised the work, Imaan thanked everyone who had helped. Mohsin showed a visitor where books should be returned. Mohsina quietly moved a box that had narrowed the walkway. Akhlaq looked at the project folder and read aloud the six lessons they had gathered: care, effort, faithfulness, gentle reminders, principled choices and service.

Then he asked Dadi one final question. “If we worked hard and did something useful, should we assume Allah has accepted it?” Dadi smiled kindly. “We hope and ask Allah to accept what is good. We do not announce that we know His unseen judgment. The Qur'an teaches that Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl asked for acceptance while they were performing a great act of obedience.”

The children stood together before their finished reading corner. No mysterious needle moved, and no door opened into the past. The compass remained in its case, a reminder that they were readers of sacred history, not visitors inside it. Yet Akhlaq felt that the journey had changed the way he looked at ordinary responsibilities.

On the final page, Sheikh Uncle had written the beginning of a new question: HOW DOES A FAMILY'S FAITH CONTINUE INTO THE NEXT GENERATION? Imaan closed the folder carefully. The Prophet Ismāʿīl's chapter had taught them to keep their word. The next world would explore another set of family lessons from the lives of the Prophets.

missions.title: The Valley and the Prayer

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Explain that Ibrāhīm prayed for his descendants and that trust in Allah includes practical care.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor

رَبَّنا إِنّى أَسكَنتُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتى بِوادٍ غَيرِ ذى زَرعٍ عِندَ بَيتِكَ المُحَرَّمِ رَبَّنا لِيُقيمُوا الصَّلوٰةَ فَاجعَل أَفـِٔدَةً مِنَ النّاسِ تَهوى إِلَيهِم وَارزُقهُم مِنَ الثَّمَرٰتِ لَعَلَّهُم يَشكُرونَ

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: Ibrāhīm says he settled some of his offspring in an uncultivated valley near Allah’s Sacred House and asks for prayer, loving hearts and provision.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

In Ibrāhīm 14:37, the Prophet prays concerning descendants settled in a valley without cultivation near Allah’s Sacred House. He asks that they establish prayer and that provision and care reach them. This Qur’anic prayer belongs beside the authentic narration of Hājar and the infant Ismāʿīl in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3364. The account teaches reliance upon Allah, but it does not turn an extraordinary command to a Prophet into a model for an ordinary parent leaving children without care. Family members and guardians bear real responsibility for children’s safety. Our modern example concerns being thoughtful about resources, making plans and helping people who depend on us.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: What is the difference between waiting for help and doing a safe action while trusting Allah?

missions.question: The neighborhood water supply has stopped. The family has safe drinking water but must allocate it carefully. Akhlaq wants to use the reserve supply to wash bicycles.

choices.text: Use the reserve water now; there looks like enough.
choices.feedback: A supply that looks plentiful may still be needed for essential use.

choices.text: Help the adults protect drinking water and postpone the bicycle wash.
choices.feedback: You protected a shared necessity and helped the family plan responsibly. Trust in Allah and good care belong together.

choices.text: Tell younger children there is no water left so they become frightened.
choices.feedback: A truthful safety plan is better than frightening or misleading children.

missions.action: Help a caregiver check and protect one shared household resource today.

remember.text: What is the difference between waiting for help and doing a safe action while trusting Allah? The learner may answer privately, choose “Think about it later,” or skip. No personal confession is required.

remember.label: Arabic recognition
remember.text: رَبَّنَا · Our Lord; وَارْزُقْهُم · and provide for them

missions.title: Seeking, Praying, and Trying

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Connect Hājar’s search described in authentic Sunnah with the Qur’anic recognition of Ṣafā and Marwah as sacred symbols.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor
إِنَّ الصَّفا وَالمَروَةَ مِن شَعائِرِ اللَّهِ ۖ فَمَن حَجَّ البَيتَ أَوِ اعتَمَرَ فَلا جُناحَ عَلَيهِ أَن يَطَّوَّفَ بِهِما ۚ وَمَن تَطَوَّعَ خَيرًا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ شاكِرٌ عَليمٌ

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: Ṣafā and Marwah are among Allah’s symbols; the verse establishes the place of movement between them in pilgrimage worship.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

Al-Baqarah 2:158 names Ṣafā and Marwah among the symbols of Allah and places movement between them within the worship connected to Ḥajj and ʿUmrah. The Qur’anic verse does not itself narrate Hājar’s seven journeys; the authentic narration in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3364 supplies that history. She acted to seek water and aid for her child, while ultimately receiving Allah’s provision. Children should not treat the school’s seven-step planning chart as a sacred formula, nor act out a pilgrimage ritual as a competition. The appropriate practical value is persistence joined to sensible action and asking adults for help when needed.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: How can a failed attempt guide my next responsible effort?

missions.question: Team Amanah’s cardboard water model falls over on the first test. Mohsin says they should stop trying and tell visitors the project was canceled.

choices.text: Give up and hide the model.
choices.feedback: A failed first attempt is information that can help us improve.

choices.text: Ask what failed, improve the design, and try again safely.
choices.feedback: You combined patient effort with learning from evidence. Honest revision is better than giving up or copying.

choices.text: Take another group’s design without credit.
choices.feedback: Taking someone else’s work does not show patient or honest effort.

missions.action: Improve one unfinished learning or household task after asking what did not work.

remember.text: How can a failed attempt guide my next responsible effort? The learner may answer privately, choose “Think about it later,” or skip. No personal confession is required.

missions.title: Learning to Care for Others

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Distinguish Hājar’s historic caregiving and the later community of Makkah from a school service project.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor

رَبَّنا إِنّى أَسكَنتُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتى بِوادٍ غَيرِ ذى زَرعٍ عِندَ بَيتِكَ المُحَرَّمِ رَبَّنا لِيُقيمُوا الصَّلوٰةَ فَاجعَل أَفـِٔدَةً مِنَ النّاسِ تَهوى إِلَيهِم وَارزُقهُم مِنَ الثَّمَرٰتِ لَعَلَّهُم يَشكُرونَ

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: Ibrāhīm says he settled some of his offspring in an uncultivated valley near Allah’s Sacred House and asks for prayer, loving hearts and provision.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

The authenticated narrative of Hājar, Zamzam and the arrival of a community shows care, divine provision and human relationships developing around the valley. Accounts about the people of Jurhum and Ismāʿīl growing up among them are preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3364; they should be taught with that attribution, rather than presented as statements found in 14:37. The Qur’an later honors Ismāʿīl independently as a truthful messenger and prophet (19:54). Our task is not to invent a detailed diary of his childhood. It is to recognize that receiving care can inspire us to become people who offer beneficial care to others.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: Who helped me learn something important, and how can I share that benefit?

missions.question: Younger students cannot read the complicated signs at the water exhibition. Akhlaq wants to keep the design because it looks impressive.

choices.text: Keep the signs and tell younger visitors to learn faster.
choices.feedback: Knowledge that humiliates a learner is not being shared well.

choices.text: Rewrite the labels clearly and help visitors understand the display.
choices.feedback: Service means making knowledge useful for the people who need it, not merely impressive for the creator.

choices.text: Remove the signs so nobody notices the problem.
choices.feedback: Hiding the problem prevents others from learning.

missions.action: Explain one useful skill kindly to someone who is learning it.

remember.text: Who helped me learn something important, and how can I share that benefit? The learner may answer privately, choose “Think about it later,” or skip. No personal confession is required.

missions.title: True to His Promise

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Recall the Qur’anic praise “true to his promise” and choose reliable conduct.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor
وَاذكُر فِى الكِتـٰبِ إِسمـٰعيلَ ۚ إِنَّهُ كانَ صادِقَ الوَعدِ وَكانَ رَسولًا نَبِيًّا

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: Allah tells us to remember Ismāʿīl in the Book: he was true to his promise and a messenger and prophet.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

Maryam 19:54 describes Ismāʿīl as صَادِقَ الْوَعْدِ, truthful to his promise, and identifies him as a messenger and prophet. This established praise is sufficient. A popular anecdote about waiting for someone for an extraordinary length of time must not be presented as a verified reason for the verse without a reliable source. A promise involves other people: someone may plan, wait, or trust because of our word. In contemporary life, reliability means making responsible commitments, keeping them when possible, communicating promptly when circumstances change, and never carrying out a harmful or unlawful promise.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: What happens to someone else when I treat my promise casually?

missions.question: Akhlaq promised to help Mohsin repair the exhibition model but wants to play football instead. Mohsin has waited for him.

choices.text: Ignore the message and hope Mohsin forgets.
choices.feedback: Silence makes another person carry the cost of a broken promise.

choices.text: Admit he forgot, apologize, and agree on a realistic time to finish together.
choices.feedback: Honesty, apology and a reliable plan repair trust. The goal is to become someone people can count on.

choices.text: Say he was sick when he was actually playing.
choices.feedback: A lie makes a missed promise worse.

missions.action: Fulfill one realistic promise today, or promptly explain if it must be rescheduled.

remember.text: What happens to someone else when I treat my promise casually? The learner may answer privately, choose “Think about it later,” or skip. No personal confession is required.

remember.label: Arabic recognition
remember.text: صَادِقَ الْوَعْدِ · true to his promise

missions.title: Encouraging Worship with Kindness

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Describe the Qur’an’s praise for Ismāʿīl’s instruction to his family in prayer and zakāh.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor
وَكانَ يَأمُرُ أَهلَهُ بِالصَّلوٰةِ وَالزَّكوٰةِ وَكانَ عِندَ رَبِّهِ مَرضِيًّا

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: Ismāʿīl used to encourage his family regarding prayer and zakāh, and he was pleasing to his Lord.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

Maryam 19:55 praises Ismāʿīl because he used to encourage his family regarding prayer and zakāh and was pleasing to his Lord. This shows that his character was not limited to private reliability: worship, responsibility and loving guidance mattered within his household. It does not justify humiliating children, spying on private worship or treating a phone alarm as proof of faith. The practical activity is helping the family make reasonable preparations for responsibilities and speaking kindly. Actual prayer obligations and developmental expectations must be taught accurately by caregivers and scholars for each age.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: How can a reminder make another person feel supported rather than judged?

missions.question: Imaan notices that Akhlaq has left his bag across the prayer space. He is rushing and dislikes being reminded.

choices.text: Call him careless in front of visitors.
choices.feedback: Public humiliation is not a good way to teach responsibility.

choices.text: Ask gently if he can move the bag and help clear the shared space.
choices.feedback: Gentle, practical help respects both worship and family relationships.

choices.text: Hide the bag to teach him a lesson.
choices.feedback: Hiding someone’s belongings creates unnecessary distress.

missions.action: Make one small, helpful preparation for family worship or a shared responsibility.

missions.title: The Patient and the Righteous

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Identify that the Qur’an counts Ismāʿīl among those distinguished by patience and righteousness.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor
وَإِسمـٰعيلَ وَإِدريسَ وَذَا الكِفلِ ۖ كُلٌّ مِنَ الصّـٰبِرينَ

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: Allah names Ismāʿīl, Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl, describing each as among those who showed patience.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85–86 names Ismāʿīl together with Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl as being among the patient and righteous, and speaks of Allah admitting them into His mercy. The passage should not be expanded into detailed incidents that have not been established. Patience in Islamic character is not indifference, passive waiting, or allowing mistreatment. For a child, it can include returning to a difficult but safe task, speaking respectfully when disappointed, or seeking help without giving up hope. Patience can also mean stepping away from unsafe behavior, rather than enduring harm silently.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: What can I do when patience means acting wisely, not simply waiting?

missions.question: Mohsina’s presentation does not work on the class projector. Other groups are waiting, and she is embarrassed.

choices.text: Blame the younger student who prepared the cables.
choices.feedback: Blaming a person without evidence is neither patient nor just.

choices.text: Ask the teacher for help, try the approved backup plan, and speak calmly.
choices.feedback: Patience makes room for honest problem-solving and appropriate help.

choices.text: Walk out without telling anybody what happened.
choices.feedback: Leaving without communication makes a solvable problem harder for others.

missions.action: When a safe task becomes difficult today, pause and try one sensible next step.

remember.text: الصَّابِرِينَ · those who are patient; الصَّالِحِينَ · the righteous

missions.title: The Great Trial and Submission

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Retell the revealed trial accurately while distinguishing the son’s identification from the literal wording of the verse.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor
رَبِّ هَب لى مِنَ الصّـٰلِحينَ

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: Ibrāhīm prays to his Lord to grant him righteous offspring.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

In al-Ṣāffāt 37:100–102, Ibrāhīm prays for righteous offspring, receives glad tidings of a forbearing boy, and later describes a dream to his son. The son answers with willingness to submit to Allah’s command. The Qur’anic passage here does not explicitly name the son; the identification with Ismāʿīl is widespread in classical Muslim explanation, with historical discussion in Tafsir. This extraordinary Prophetic event cannot be recreated or used to justify endangering any child. The accessible moral application is to prefer truth, care and legitimate obedience over boastfulness or selfish comfort while protecting every child’s safety.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: When has being recognized felt more important to me than doing what is right?

missions.question: Team Amanah is organizing donated supplies. Akhlaq wants his name on the largest banner although many students worked.

choices.text: Take full credit because he spent the most time.
choices.feedback: Taking credit from others is not justified by working hard.

choices.text: Give fair credit and make the service purpose more visible than his own name.
choices.feedback: The difficult right choice here is a modest, safe act of fairness; it is not a reenactment of the Prophetic trial.

choices.text: Delete the other students’ names.
choices.feedback: Erasing contributors violates fairness and trust.

missions.action: Give proper credit to one person who helped with a shared task.

remember.text: When has being recognized felt more important to me than doing what is right? The learner may answer privately, choose “Think about it later,” or skip. No personal confession is required.

remember.label: Arabic recognition
remember.text: إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ · if Allah wills; الصَّابِرِينَ · the patient

missions.title: Relief from Allah and the Meaning of the Test

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Explain that Allah supplied a great ransom and that worship is not measured by display.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor
فَلَمّا أَسلَما وَتَلَّهُ لِلجَبينِ

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: The father and son submitted, and Ibrāhīm laid the son down as described in the verse.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

The Qur’an states that Ibrāhīm and the son submitted, that Allah called Ibrāhīm, declared the vision fulfilled, identified the event as a clear trial, and ransomed the son with a great sacrifice (37:103–107). All of that belongs to a unique revealed history. Al-Ḥajj 22:37 separately teaches that the meat and blood of sacrificial animals do not reach Allah; rather, piety does. We must not convert this into an exercise asking a child to face danger, harm an animal, prove belief through pain, or keep frightening secrets. Religious rites belong within their lawful rules and adult supervision. For the app, the safe character lesson concerns sincere intentions and doing good without demanding applause.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: Would I still choose this good action if nobody praised me?

missions.question: Akhlaq wants to announce every item he donated because he hopes the teacher will praise him.

choices.text: Only help if the teacher promises a public reward.
choices.feedback: Making praise a condition weakens the service intention.

choices.text: Contribute what he can sincerely and thank the other helpers.
choices.feedback: The purpose of the good deed matters more than applause. A sincere action does not need a show.

choices.text: Tell classmates he donated things he did not actually give.
choices.feedback: Claiming other people’s donations is dishonest.

missions.action: Do one small good deed today without demanding public recognition.

remember.text: Would I still choose this good action if nobody praised me? The learner may answer privately, choose “Think about it later,” or skip. No personal confession is required.

remember.label: Arabic recognition
remember.text: وَفَدَيْنَاهُ · and We ransomed him; التَّقْوَىٰ · piety

missions.title: Raising the Foundations Together

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Identify Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl as the named builders raising the foundations of the Sacred House.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor

وَإِذ جَعَلنَا البَيتَ مَثابَةً لِلنّاسِ وَأَمنًا وَاتَّخِذوا مِن مَقامِ إِبرٰهـۧمَ مُصَلًّى ۖ وَعَهِدنا إِلىٰ إِبرٰهـۧمَ وَإِسمـٰعيلَ أَن طَهِّرا بَيتِىَ لِلطّائِفينَ وَالعـٰكِفينَ وَالرُّكَّعِ السُّجودِ

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: Allah appointed the House as a place of return and security; Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl were commanded regarding its purification for worship.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

Al-Baqarah 2:127 names Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl together raising the foundations of the House while asking Allah to accept their work. Al-Baqarah 2:125 sets the Sacred House within worship and purification. The Qur’an teaches a real, uniquely sacred event; an ordinary school building is neither the Kaʿbah nor an imitation of its ritual status. The ethical application is cooperation, dividing useful tasks, respecting differing abilities, and ensuring that a shared project serves its intended purpose. The authenticated Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3364 narrative gives further context on father and son working together; any dialogue quoted must remain accurately attributed.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: Am I focused on the purpose of our work or only on being noticed?

missions.question: Team Amanah must improve the school reading corner. Akhlaq wants decorative towers; Imaan is concerned that younger children cannot reach the books.

choices.text: Build only the impressive towers.
choices.feedback: A beautiful feature is not enough when the project fails the people it should serve.

choices.text: Prioritize safe shelves, clear paths and useful reading space while sharing the work.
choices.feedback: A thoughtful team builds something useful for others and gives every helper a meaningful role.

choices.text: Let one child do all the work so it is finished faster.
choices.feedback: Teamwork means sharing responsibility rather than overburdening one learner.

missions.action: Cooperate with someone on one useful shared task today.

remember.text: Am I focused on the purpose of our work or only on being noticed? The learner may answer privately, choose “Think about it later,” or skip. No personal confession is required.

missions.title: Our Lord, Accept from Us

discover.label: Learning objective
discover.text: Understand that the builders asked for acceptance, submission and guidance beyond their own lives.
READ — The Qur’anic anchor
رَبَّنا وَاجعَلنا مُسلِمَينِ لَكَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسلِمَةً لَكَ وَأَرِنا مَناسِكَنا وَتُب عَلَينا ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ التَّوّابُ الرَّحيمُ

discover.label: Child-friendly meaning
discover.text: They prayed for submission to Allah, for submission among their descendants, for guidance in rites and for repentance.
UNDERSTAND — The meaning and context

After the foundations are raised, the Qur’an records Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl asking Allah to make them submissive to Him, guide their descendants in worship, accept their repentance, and raise among their descendants a messenger who would recite Allah’s signs and teach them the Book and wisdom (al-Baqarah 2:128–129). We learn that great work should lead toward humility and prayer, not the claim that we know our action has been accepted in the unseen. The source points beyond a single generation: families teach through words, mercy, example and responsible service. A classroom reading corner is a contemporary application only; its purpose and rank are not those of the Kaʿbah.
A MOMENT TO REFLECT

discover.label: Think about the lesson before making a choice
discover.text: What good habit could remain useful after I finish this mission?

missions.question: The new reading corner opens. A teacher praises the team, and Akhlaq is tempted to say the project was perfect and that everyone must thank him.

choices.text: Say their work proves they are better than other teams.
choices.feedback: Comparisons and boasting do not make a good action better.

choices.text: Thank everyone, ask Allah to accept sincere efforts, and listen to ideas for improvement.
choices.feedback: Gratitude and humility help good work continue benefiting others. We seek Allah’s acceptance rather than declaring it certain.

choices.text: Refuse to let anyone suggest a change.
choices.feedback: Listening to improvements helps the project keep serving others.

missions.action: Thank one contributor to a shared good effort and make one modest improvement.

remember.text: What good habit could remain useful after I finish this mission? The learner may answer privately, choose “Think about it later,” or skip. No personal confession is required.

review.meaning: Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl raised the foundations of the House and asked Allah to accept their work.

review.meaning: They prayed for submission to Allah, for submission among their descendants, for guidance in rites and for repentance.

review.meaning: They prayed that a messenger from among their descendants would recite Allah’s signs and teach the Book and wisdom and purify the people.

synthesis.text: The journey from receiving care to carrying a trust

The child Ismāʿīl’s earliest account reminds us that life begins with dependence. His mother Hājar cared for him in a profoundly difficult circumstance preserved by the authentic Sunnah. Allah’s provision through Zamzam was mercy, not an invitation for human beings to manufacture danger in order to demand a miracle. The children’s first task, therefore, is to understand that reliance upon Allah goes with practical care, truthful planning and responsible protection of those entrusted to us.

The Qur’an then gives Ismāʿīl a remarkable independent distinction: he was a messenger and prophet, true to his promise (19:54). Reliability is not merely a pleasing social habit. It guards the rights and expectations of others. The promise that is forgotten may leave another person waiting, carrying an unfair workload or doubting whether our word means anything. For that reason, the mission challenges never ask children to make grand vows. They teach manageable commitments, clear communication and honest repair.

The next words of Maryam praise Ismāʿīl for reminding his household of prayer and zakāh. His example links religion with family life and the way people care for those around them. A gentle reminder is different from surveillance, and spiritual instruction is different from humiliation. Together with the Qur’an’s praise of his patience and righteousness in al-Anbiyāʾ, the account shows a character formed through steady acts rather than public excitement.

The great trial described in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt is not a classroom challenge. It is a unique revealed history, whose details must be preserved as revelation states them and interpreted through sound scholarship. The son’s acceptance, Allah’s declaration that the trial was fulfilled, and the great ransom carry religious meaning that no invented school competition can replicate. The practical teaching for children must always be safe: truthfulness, lawful obedience, sincerity and courage to do what is right without hurting anyone.

Finally, the valley of dependence becomes a place of lasting worship. Al-Baqarah 2:127 names Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl as they raised the foundations of the House. Even while working, they prayed for acceptance. The following verses extend their prayer beyond themselves, toward worship, repentance and a future Messenger who would teach Allah’s guidance. A child learns from this humility: do useful work, thank those who help, ask Allah to accept sincere efforts, and consider what good habit may benefit the next person.
Five values to carry into the next world
1. Trust with action. Rely upon Allah and take safe, responsible steps rather than abandoning your duties.
2. Truthfulness in promises. Give only commitments you can responsibly honor; communicate when you cannot.
3. Patient and gentle responsibility. Work through difficulty, seek help and speak respectfully to those who learn with you.
4. Sincerity over display. Choose beneficial actions without needing applause or invented spiritual scores.
5. Service that continues. Cooperate to make a useful improvement that others can maintain and enjoy.
